newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds marked up on rumours but volume thin.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds marked up on rumours but volume thin.

text.p: Irish bonds were marked up in price on Tuesday, fuelled by persistent currency valuation rumours, but volumes remained thin, dealers said.
"The revaluation story that's going around is obviously market-supportive and there's a small amount of buying interest on the margins," a dealer said.
"But I don't believe there's anything in it - a currency revaluation in the short term just doesn't add up."
By 1445 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was up 35 pence at 102.52 to yield 5.81 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was up 38 pence at 110.13 to yield 6.49 percent.
Irish bonds outperformed Germany on Tuesday, with yields against Bunds narrowing slightly from Monday's close to 150 basis points over in the five-year bond, and 91 over in the 10-year.

In morning trade on Tuesday the Irish pound hovered around 2.64 marks and 0.91 sterling, underpinned by the revaluation story, although foreign exchange dealers were also sceptical of an imminent move.
One foreign exchange dealer said rumours that the Irish pound would be revalued probably originated in bond market speculation.

Forex dealers believe the new Irish government would be reluctant to rush into a revaluation as it could leave the Irish economy very vulnerable to a sterling depreciation at a later date and would upset Irish exporters and farmers, two strong lobby groups.
Revaluing the punt at this stage might also be in breach of the rules governing a single currency, they say.

The government is more likely to wait, hoping that EU officials opt for conversion at average rates as this would be an effective revaluation, allowing Ireland to stay within the Maastricht rules and without the need to take a politically tough decision, a dealer said.
Bond dealers have complained that the weak punt has been causing Irish bonds to underperform against Spain and Italy over recent weeks.
Meanwhile market focus on Tuesday will be the release of the NAPM index in the U.S. and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) which begins a two-day meeting to discuss interest rates.
Dealers are also waiting for UK Chancellor Gordon Brown's first budget tomorrow to see how tight a fiscal package he announces and its impact on sterling.

At home EBR figures on Wednesday and credit data on Thursday will be watched, particularly EBR which is likely to show a large budget surplus at mid-year and emphasise that there will be limited issuance of fresh stock over the balance of the year.
There is expectation in the market that the National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) will issue a statement about supply later in the week.
